issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost Community and culture' is not impossible for a combat trauma survivor, but for a 49-year-old married male European city council member it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile and is weakly anchored to the rest of the selected nodes. The rest of the profile centers on bodily danger, touch/startle, fragmented trauma recall, and safety distrust; this item instead implies a culturally/community dislocation theme that is not supported elsewhere in Triggers/Threat/Memory/Maladaptive Strategies.

issues.item: Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
issues.explanation: 'Overwhelming grief on recall' is not inherently inconsistent, but here it is the least coherent memory item relative to the formulation and other selected items. The profile is dominated by fear-based threat, bodily vulnerability, touch alarm, and cognitive disorganization of recall. A grief-dominant recall item without corresponding loss/bereavement appraisals or related strategies makes the memory cluster less internally aligned.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The profile is largely coherent for a middle-aged male combat survivor, but this appraisal is the main mismatch. 'My body has been permanently damaged' implies a salient lasting physical injury. That idea is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile: memory items focus on fragmented, terror-laden recall; threat items emphasize current danger, mistrust of safety, startle to touch, and sleep disturbance; maladaptive strategies emphasize sensory distraction, thought monitoring, and avoidance of touch. There are no triggers selected, and no other items indicate ongoing medical consequences or trauma themes centered on bodily injury. In this profile, the appraisal reads as if it belongs to a different subtype centered on physical injury rather than the represented combat-related fear/terror formulation.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile in a 49-year-old male, this specific self-blame item is the main coherence problem. The rest of the profile centers on persistent danger, touch-triggered alarm, fragmented/terror-laden memory, and defensive avoidance, which fits combat-related PTSD. In contrast, 'the event happened because of the way I acted' implies a strong internal-causal guilt formulation that is not otherwise supported by the selected memory, threat, or strategy items. This makes the appraisal set less coherent with the overall profile and with the formulation, where Memory and Threat strongly feed Negative Appraisals focused on ongoing danger rather than responsibility for causing the trauma. Self-blame can occur in combat PTSD, but here it is insufficiently connected to the other selected items and stands out as the least clinically coherent item.

vignette: John is a 49-year-old European-American City Council Member who served in combat and has been struggling with the aftermath of his traumatic experiences. Despite being married, John finds himself increasingly isolated from those around him due to the intense fears and intrusive memories that plague him daily. The trauma began during his time in combat when he witnessed and experienced events that left deep emotional scars. He often feels like parts of these memories are missing or unclear, making it hard for him to piece together a coherent picture of what happened. When John tries to recount these experiences, the narrative frequently falters, leaving him feeling frustrated and unable to explain the full scope of his trauma. This incomplete recollection exacerbates his distress because he is constantly left wondering about the details that are missing. This fragmented memory contributes significantly to his maladaptive strategies. Whenever he feels overwhelmed by intrusive thoughts or triggered by reminders of his combat experiences, John often turns up the volume on loud music or TV, seeking to drown out the overwhelming sensations and regain a sense of control. He has also become hypervigilant, constantly monitoring his own thoughts for signs that he is going crazy. This constant mental vigilance only adds to his stress, making it difficult for him to relax and trust his surroundings. John's memories are so potent that they often lead to startle responses whenever someone touches him unexpectedly. Despite being in a safe environment, like his home or office, John cannot shake the feeling of danger. His wife has noticed how he flinches at even gentle touches, a reaction that strains their relationship and makes it hard for her to comfort him. The incomplete memories also fuel his negative appraisals about himself and the world around him. He believes that his body is an enemy, constantly reacting as if he were still in danger. This constant state of hypervigilance has led him to distrust the safety others assure him exists. Even when people tell John he is safe, he finds it impossible to believe them because his body and mind are convinced otherwise. John's maladaptive strategies have further entrenched these negative appraisals and memories. His reliance on sensory distraction to cope with intrusive thoughts only serves to amplify the fear and disconnection he feels. When he turns up the volume or distracts himself, the memories resurface even more vividly, making it difficult for him to trust that he is truly safe. The cycle of hypervigilance and memory distortion has significantly impacted his life as a City Council Member. John often finds himself avoiding social engagements and public appearances where physical contact might be expected or where he could be triggered by the crowded, unpredictable environments typical in city governance settings. His decision to avoid these situations stems from the fear that he cannot trust others' assurances of safety. What finally brought John to seek help is the increasing isolation and strain on his marriage. He fears being trapped in this cycle indefinitely, unable to fully engage with life or reconnect with those around him. While he hopes for relief from his intrusive memories and a sense of safety, what frightens him most is the uncertainty about whether he can ever truly believe that he is safe. John's journey towards recovery will involve addressing these interconnected symptoms, breaking the cycle of negative appraisals, and finding healthier ways to cope with his traumatic memories.
